title: National Tire Dealers & Retreaders Association, Inc. v. Brinegar
lead: Retreaders contest the burden of permanent tire labels, and a partial vacatur separates Congress’s own labeling commands from inadequately justified agency additions.

actors.name: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA)
actors.role: Agency adopting passenger-tire retreading Standard No. 117.

actors.name: Secretary of Transportation
actors.role: Respondent defending the agency’s safety and practicability determinations.

proceedings: NHTSA adopted the labeling provision after informal proposals, a technical conference, and reconsideration.
The association petitioned directly for D.C. Circuit review.
The court vacated discretionary permanence requirements in part, preserving Congress’s express commands; Robinson concurred on practicability grounds.
limits: The court did not invalidate all Standard No. 117 or certify industry cost predictions universally. The majority’s safety rationale was not Robinson’s basis, and legislative labeling commands remained binding despite agency disagreement.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The new rule requires variable information on retreaded casings
sections.cue: Why was permanence difficult for the industry?
paragraphs: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration adopted Standard No. 117 under the 1966 motor-vehicle safety statute. Paragraph S6.3.2 required passenger tires retreaded from February 1, 1974, to bear permanently molded sidewall information: size, maximum inflation, maximum load, actual ply number or ply rating, tube type, and applicable bias-belted or radial construction.

Retreaders reused many casing sizes and constructions. Buffing old tread could erase shoulder markings, and only about one-third of existing casings retained all needed information. A July 1, 1973 new-tire labeling amendment placed markings where they would survive retreading, but replacement of old inventory would take time.

Limiting production to marked casings could sharply reduce output. Relabeling others required repeated changes of information plates in hot molds. Industry comments described many combinations, burns, expense, and failed labels. One experiment reported eighty-percent effectiveness and over $2.50 extra per retread, roughly thirty percent. These were submissions raising doubts, not universally established cost findings.

sources.pinpoint: Facts and agency action; Parts I, III; nn.1–3, 30–39

sections.title: The agency invokes existing methods and expertise; the association seeks review
sections.cue: Which statutory choices constrained the review?
paragraphs: The association argued affixed labels could inform buyers without permanence’s burden. NHTSA thought identification and recordkeeping techniques adaptable and suggested sorting casings to reduce plate changes. Its reconsideration denial invoked available information and expertise while disclaiming a need to link particular records to determinations.

The agency had used informal notice and comment with a technical conference, proposals, and reconsideration. The association did not demand formal procedure. The D.C. Circuit used Automotive Parts’ approach: searching arbitrary-and-capricious examination of legislative materials, not mandatory formal substantial-evidence review.

Section 103 required objective standards meeting safety needs and economic practicability. Legislative history included reasonable cost, feasibility, and lead time, not technological possibility alone. Section 201 separately commanded permanent, conspicuous tire information including actual ply number and maximum load. Actual ply number differed from discretionary ply rating, which mattered to the eventual remedy.

sources.pinpoint: Agency response; Procedure and statute; nn.10–13, 26–29

sections.title: Wilkey questions the added safety value of permanent information
sections.cue: What had to be shown beyond usefulness at the sale?
paragraphs: Judge Wilkey, joined by Tamm, accepted the safety value of information preventing mismatching, overload, and overinflation. Permanence was the issue: a temporary affixed label could inform the first purchaser. Later vehicle transfers, resale, or replacement matching might justify lasting information, but the Secretary supplied no record illustrations showing their frequency and significance.

The majority could imagine scenarios but would not supply their importance itself. Government acknowledgment that an expert could identify many characteristics by inspection weakened unexplained necessity further. The additional relationship was too remote on this record for the asserted burdens; labels generally were not declared useless.

Congress’s own actual-ply and maximum-load commands nevertheless survived. Judicial review of discretionary agency choices could not reweigh Congress’s explicit selection. Saying administrative-procedure tests did not govern Congress did not immunize statutes from all constitutional review.

sources.pinpoint: Majority safety analysis; Part II; nn.17–24

sections.title: Unsupported feasibility assurances do not answer concrete contrary submissions
sections.cue: Why did the identification-label analogy fall short?
paragraphs: The agency could use expertise and its files, and the court need not accept every interested prediction. But serious, specific burdens required support, persuasive explanation, or an inherently plausible answer.

Retreader identity remained largely constant, and production-week markings changed weekly with cool molds. This safety information varied casing by casing. A working method for stable information did not establish economic feasibility for frequent changes. Sorting sounded plausible but lacked evidence of practicability and reasonable price. Refusing to connect supporting records to conclusions aggravated the explanatory gap.
Under APA § 706(2)(A), the discretionary permanent-label additions were arbitrary on this record. The court did not foreclose a supported future requirement based on better evidence and reasoning.

sections.title: Robinson accepts the safety connection but agrees that costs were not addressed
sections.cue: Which requirements fell, and which did Congress require?
paragraphs: Judge Spottswood W. Robinson III concurred in disposition on economic practicability. Continued label value across wheel and vehicle transfers was sufficiently apparent from common experience, and technological feasibility was undisputed. He therefore rejected the majority’s safety doubts.

About thirty million tires were retreaded yearly, with an estimated twenty million lacking proper surviving marks. Numerous combinations demanded slug changes and affected both businesses and motorists relying on affordable retreads. Robinson found no adequate economic analysis supporting these burdens. That narrower ground, rather than the whole safety discussion, explained all judges’ agreement.

On January 8, 1974, the court vacated permanent labeling of size, maximum inflation, ply rating, tube type, and applicable construction designation. It preserved Congress’s actual-ply and maximum-load requirements: Standard No. 117 was vacated only in part. Judicial notes also identified Congress’s command of permanent ply-material composition labeling, which NHTSA had omitted as insufficiently safety-related. The agency could not replace that legislative judgment with its own. Remaining commands might still be costly but involved fewer items; the court did not draft a replacement rule.

The comparison with Automotive Parts concerns the same serious informal review reaching different results because record explanations differed. This account addresses the historical rule, not present tire requirements.

sources.pinpoint: Robinson concurrence 41–43 & nn.1–11; Judgment; majority nn.6, 45
